received_record.context_summary: Fallon notes that the account had two Google campaigns spending $60 per day and asks whether Lauren wants to reduce that as Meta is added. Lauren says spend has risen and traffic increased, but she has not yet seen clearly stronger leads; she is open to testing and wants the team's recommendation. Whitney explains that the team typically begins with an even Google/Meta split until data gives a basis for reallocating, and says dropping Google from $60 per day to about $16.66 would be drastic. She proposes roughly $1,000 per month ($30 per day) as a fresh-campaign starting point, partly to avoid an abrupt cut and test a lower budget. Lauren agrees. Fallon later says they can monitor and revisit allocation in reports and ongoing communication.
received_record.proposition: After Lauren raises budget concerns and questions how to divide spend across Google and Meta, Whitney recommends starting Google at about $1,000 per month rather than reducing it immediately to the $500-per-month minimum, explaining the proposed split and the risk of a drastic reduction. Lauren agrees to the starting point; later monitoring and reallocation are described as future work.
received_record.audience_relevance: Owners weighing ad budgets across channels may have to reconcile rising spend, increased traffic, and uncertain lead quality. The exchange shows how a recommendation can respond to both the client's evidence and the implications of changing budgets while adding a channel.
qualifications: The recommendation and client agreement do not establish that the budget was implemented or that it improved results.
Whitney's suggestion that rising Google budgets can inflate cost per lead is presented as a possibility, not a demonstrated cause in this account.
The recorded spend amounts and proposed allocation relate to this specific account, not a general benchmark.
reasons: The client raises a decision-relevant concern, asks for guidance, and contributes observations; the team explains its recommendation rather than simply prescribing a fixed split.
The exchange reveals that a budget decision was framed as a starting point to monitor, not a promised performance outcome.

discovery.wia_contribution: Fallon reviews the existing Google spend and asks about budget comfort; Whitney explains the initial channel split and recommends a less abrupt Google reduction, with monitoring and later reallocation described as the next step.
discovery.attention_reason: The moment can demonstrate judgment under uncertainty: the team responds to the client's concern without treating either the previous spend or a default minimum as automatically correct.
research_questions: Was the proposed budget implemented, and what did later account data show?
How was the combined Google and Meta budget ultimately set and monitored?

received_record.quote: I have my own systems all built out
received_record.context_summary: Whitney asks about Ivor's advertising history and what kind of support he wants. Ivor explains that he runs the business, ads, and lead handling himself; he has built an automated self-service flow and says most customers move through it without direct intervention. He is seeking ongoing strategic support and better ad efficiency, not basic CRM setup. Whitney recognizes the infrastructure, explains that WIA can assess his existing systems and work consultatively on landing pages, while describing LeadLock as an option rather than a necessity. She also asks for client-side lead and booking information so WIA can collaborate with his existing knowledge. This was a consultation; the recording does not establish a purchase or subsequent work.
received_record.proposition: Ivor describes an established, largely self-built lead and booking system and says he is seeking more efficient advertising and ongoing strategic support. Whitney acknowledges that his back-end systems are already in place, distinguishes consultative landing-page advice from a LeadLock-supported build, and describes client collaboration around downstream lead and booking information.
received_record.audience_relevance: Established owners may already have capable operational systems and still want expert advertising support. The exchange models assessing the specific gap rather than assuming every prospective client needs the same CRM or funnel setup.
qualifications: Ivor's claims about the share of customers moving through his automated flow are his report, not independently verified measurements.
The conversation is a consultation and does not establish that Ivor became a client or that any recommendation was implemented.
Whitney describes possible work and options in this sales conversation; it does not by itself establish current service scope.
reasons: The prospect gives a detailed account of his existing capability, and Whitney adjusts the discussion rather than positioning a system he says he does not need.
The exchange reveals a broader fit principle: useful advertising support can complement a capable owner's existing process, with collaboration focused on the actual unresolved problem.

discovery.wia_contribution: Whitney asks about the owner's existing systems and goals, recognizes his operational infrastructure, and distinguishes consultative input from a LeadLock-based build while emphasizing shared downstream information.
discovery.attention_reason: This challenges the assumption that an owner seeking ad help must first replace a working back-end system. It may help qualified prospects understand how support can be tailored to existing capabilities rather than sold as a one-size-fits-all setup.
research_questions: Did this prospect proceed, and what scope of work, if any, was ultimately agreed?
How did WIA define the division of responsibility for existing landing pages, lead handling, and reporting in any subsequent work?
